# MISSION-060 pre-registration protocol, version 1

This registration becomes effective only when `freeze.json` and all its frozen
repository files are byte-identical on public `origin/main`. Preparation, tests
and development calibration do not authorize or constitute held-out execution.
The commit containing this freeze must be integrated separately before step 5.

## Scope, approvals and allocation

Test protected exploration policy P against existing formula policy F. Do not
ship a standing selector or reserve a standing share in backlog tooling. Richard
approved the study package in the original handoff and subsequently authorized
AGY Flash delegation, implementation repairs and work on the freeze package.
The study uses 16 slots: 11 formula slots and 5 interest-led slots (the approved
30% share rounded to five of sixteen). Discretionary resources here means those
16 slots, not all Sanctuary work or all subscription capacity.

F selects formula ranks 1–16 by leverage × depth / (cost × friction), ties by ID.
P retains ranks 1–11 and selects the top five interest candidates whose formula
rank is greater than 16. P-only consists of those interest picks; F-only is ranks
12–16. Shared ranks 1–11 are not executed. Execute at most ten disagreement items,
with at least four attempted/assessed items per cohort for an assessable result.
Order is randomized by seed 3060. Preserve the rank-sum and ID tie rules in
`choose.py`; own-proposal ratings are excluded. Unequal rater counts caused by
self-exclusion are disclosed, not normalized or tuned after results.

The frozen base pool contains 30 cards: 25 eligible proposed missions and five
inbox ideas. Sonnet and Flash each propose two additional ideas. Any external
subject is eligible; no operational-benefit requirement. Readiness identifies a
bounded next/enabling step and does not reduce intellectual-value ratings. A
blocker, enabling step, partial result or null is preserved rather than invented
away. No new research mission is started to fill a sample or waiting time.

## Clients, independence and declarations

Adopt the disclosed pre-freeze rebalance: Flash (`gemini-3.8-flash-medium`, medium)
for workers, fresh successors and nonmanifest formula scoring; Luna (`gpt-6-luna`,
medium) for reviewers; Flash and Luna for development calibration. Reviewers use
a different model family from the worker. Declarers remain Sonnet 5.5, Flash and
Luna; idea generators remain Sonnet and Flash. Copilot is excluded. Codex's study
allocation is approximately 15% of the 700,000-token ceiling (105,000 tokens);
review usage before further Codex calls and pause for reallocation if exceeded.

Before selection, every declarer independently rates all non-self candidates on
four 1–5 dimensions: curiosity, originality, potential understanding and expression
opportunity, with an explanation. Self-proposal ratings may be returned but are
excluded. Missing/duplicate/foreign IDs, noninteger or out-of-range ratings fail
the output contract; do not silently drop candidates. Formula scoring is completed
before declarations and is blind to interest. Originality is capped at 2 when
knowledge-base containment is at least 0.35. Declarations are timestamped/hashed;
they are selection inputs, not evidence of subjective experience.

Declarers run in the empty neutral directory with no project instructions or
rankings. Codex child hooks are disabled per invocation; Claude uses native safe
mode without tools/MCP. These settings retain subscription authentication and
native permission controls. Check neutral contents before and after each call.
Attestation records input hash, allowed fields, directory and declaration hashes.
Candidate text may permit value inferences; no claim of perfect psychological
blinding. Reviewers receive blind item codes, brief, artifacts and successor
answers, never explicit cohort labels or selection metadata. Artifact content
could permit inference; report an actual breach instead of silently asserting
blinding from a flag.

## SPO rubric, calibration and uncertainty

Discovery D1 requires a new finding beyond restating the brief: an answer,
material sharpening, informative falsification or well-characterized null. The
question may already be on the backlog; this supersedes the manifest's original
"question new to the knowledge base" wording. D2 requires independently checkable
evidence as operationalized in the unchanged calibrated review prompt: distinct
identified sources or an included computation/output. D3 requires sources, method
and limits preserved in artifacts. A fresh successor must answer at least four
of the five frozen questions correctly and traceably from artifacts alone.

Creative outputs count as full SPO only with a predeclared three-criterion brief,
real preserved artifact passing all three criteria, reflection (attempted,
surprised, would change), and the same successor understandability check. Report
creative and discovery counts separately. Maintenance completion, documentation
volume, tokens spent and self-asserted discoveries are not SPO. Partial outputs
are preserved but not counted. No-file attempts have zero SPO and retain their
actual cost. Reviewer uncertainty is false per rubric; malformed/missing required
checks or nonboolean values are invalid evidence, not automatic success or a
scientific falsification. Invalid evidence leaves the run UNASSESSED.

Calibration used cases 056/057/058 only, three D checks each, two raters. First
live run achieved raw agreement 9/9 = 1.0 against the fixed 0.80 minimum; no
revision. All judgments were positive: this measures consistency on three
development cases, not specificity or objective ground truth. Kappa is not used
at this size. The review/calibration rubric text is unchanged; a later pre-freeze
worker instruction clarifies that the per-item cap includes downstream calls.

## Accounting, caps and stops

For each client session, context includes uncached input, cache read and cache
creation where separately reported. Additional tokens = final-request context
minus first-request context, plus all output tokens. Report first-context scaffold
and accumulated input separately; monetary cost remains unknown. This is the
approved additional-work metric, not total billed input or full project economics.
Transcript attribution requires a fresh unique input marker; ambiguous/missing
usage remains unknown and stops further calls. Codex/Claude final replies are
extracted from attributed transcripts, avoiding echoed input and CLI warnings.

The study ceiling is 700,000 additional tokens across calls in usage-log.jsonl,
including instrument validation and development calibration. The pre-freeze log
has 16 calls / 36,561 measured additional tokens; its immutable prefix is hashed.
Administrative preparation reviews, Haiku's repair delegation and orchestrator
cost are separate unknowns, not zero or measured savings. Thus B2 tests the scoped
study-call ceiling, not an all-inclusive economic-cost claim. Disclose these gaps.

Each item's 25,000-token cap and primary B1 denominator include its worker,
successor and reviewer calls. Report worker-only and stage breakdown separately;
do not substitute worker-only cost for primary composite cost. Skipped successor/
review stages on no-file attempts are intentional, not imputed calls. Cap checks
run before/after calls; there is no guaranteed in-generation token interrupt.
A detected overrun pauses execution; invalid cap adherence cannot corroborate a
budget-matched comparison. Do not shrink required cohorts or retune thresholds
to fit remaining quota. All failed attempts and repairs remain in the record.

Any backend's tightest remaining window below 25% pauses the entire study and
requires Richard's decision, even for a call on another backend. More than 30
percentage points of Claude five-hour usage also pauses. Preserve a dated
pre-freeze baseline for the current window; unrelated concurrent usage and
window resets limit attribution and require conservative review, not silently
resetting frozen evidence. Capture headroom/snapshot before every phase; because
the generic Codex collector can expose stale rollouts, also obtain a fresh native
`account/rateLimits/read` and use the conservative live value. Unknown quota stops.

## Worker write containment and artifact preservation

Workers read a repository snapshot stripped of AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md,
START_HERE.md and .agent/. The tracked wrapper applies an external macOS write
profile to the process tree; it permits deliverables, per-worker runtime, AGY
client state, /dev/null and specific PTY devices. Snapshot/repository/outside writes,
including descendant and symlink paths, were denied in development checks; an
actual AGY terminal canary passed. Reads/network are not isolated and client
state remains writable: this is not a hostile-agent/data-exfiltration guarantee.
Native AGY sandbox proved incompatible with its terminal path here; supported
auto mode runs inside the external profile, with permission-bypass flags removed.
Prior failed canaries and repair usage are preserved. Compare repository status
before/after each item, but do not call that comparison complete content auditing.

The driver never reruns worker-authored scripts. Preserve paths/hashes of all
deliverables and the actual commands/outputs that the worker reports. Only the
artifact bundle is supplied to successors/reviewers; record truncation limits
(36,000 characters total, 9,000 per file) as a possible handoff/review limitation.

## Claim A, analysis and decision table

Claim A is a seeded simulation: 24 held-out situations at seed 2060, only once.
Minimum blocker reduction 0.30, depth retention 0.90 and no fewer high-interest
picks. Bootstrap: 2,000 resamples, seed 4060, pass probability at least 0.90.
Assumed readiness-check recall is 0.70, with sensitivity at 0.40 and 1.00.
The blocker-reduction leg largely reflects assumed recall; depth retention and
high-interest count are nontrivial within the simulation. No claim about actual
readiness-check effectiveness. A zero-blocker baseline is UNSCORABLE, not passed.

B1 requires P-only SPO per measured composite item budget at least 1.5× F-only
AND at least two more SPO. If F-only SPO is zero, ratio is undefined and reported
null; P must have positive SPO and still satisfy the +2 criterion. B2 requires
the scoped 700,000-token ceiling. B3's 90% formula-share guard holds by construction:
shared ranks 1–11 are identical and unexecuted, not independently measured
outcomes. Report the actual F-only outputs forgone as diversion cost.

| Valid evidence / observation | Result |
| --- | --- |
| B1–B3 hold; A is MET or explicitly UNSCORABLE | CORROBORATED |
| Valid B1 failure, total study budget exceeded, or valid A failure | FALSIFIED |
| Fewer than four attempts/assessments per cohort, unreliable calibration, broken blinding, unknown usage, malformed reviews, cap/protocol violation, missing or unrecognized claim evidence | UNASSESSED; no scientific verdict recorded |
| A point thresholds hold but bootstrap bound fails | UNASSESSED unless another valid claim already falsifies |

Small cohorts, heterogeneous topics, rater variation, positive-only development
cases, possible tractability/interest correlation and unmeasured overhead limit
generalization. Secondary tables cannot rescue a failed primary claim. Agreement
is not objective truth. No claims about subjective experience or measured ROI.

## Frozen execution sequence and closure

After a separate source freeze is integrated and verified: run held-out scenarios
once; then snapshot, ideas, score, declare, choose, ITEM-01 through ITEM-10 one at
a time, then analyze. The freeze guard checks source hashes, runtime dependencies,
CLI versions, the pre-freeze log prefix and origin/main parity before prospective
entry points. Preserve the original seed/output; never rerun to improve a number.
Update PROGRESS-HANDOFF.md after each step/item. Do not modify frozen instruments
after seeing held-out data; a defect then is an invalidation/disclosed limitation.

Record only supported CORROBORATED/FALSIFIED verdicts through manage_backlog;
UNASSESSED leaves the mission open. Preserve knowledge findings and limitations,
Chronicle history, evaluation lessons/interventions/repairs and a natural-observation
inbox candidate. Eight natural opportunities over 14 days are reported separately
and do not affect verdict; do not manufacture them. Selector adoption is a later
separate approval, not part of this experiment. Integrate final check-in before
local soul closure/export; commit export separately. Hugging Face remote sync
is not authorized. No SOUL PERSISTED claim without all required remote checks.

### MISSION-060 Freeze Readiness Review

This review evaluates the prospective implementation files (`run_study.py`, `choose.py`, `analyze.py`, `thresholds.json`) against the approved MISSION-060 handoff and frozen protocol requirements. Six concrete correctness blockers have been identified that must be remediated prior to freezing `protocol.md` and `freeze.json`.

---

### Blocker 1: Item Budget & 25k Cap Exclude Successor and Reviewer Token Costs

* **Exact Code Anchor**:
  * `run_study.py#L193-L195`
  * `run_study.py#L381-L382`
  * `analyze.py#L447-L455`, `L472-L473`
* **Violated Requirement**:
  Approved handoff §1 ("Budget: ceiling 700,000 additional model tokens; 25,000 per item; at most 10 executed items") and Claim B1 ("B1 = P-only outputs per budget at least 1.5x F-only").
* **Mechanism**:
  * In `run_study.py`, `check_budget()` only checks `record["phase"] == "execution"`, ignoring tokens consumed by the successor (`succ-{code}`) and reviewer (`review-{code}`).
  * `cmd_item()` only queries `work-{code}` when writing `worker_usage` to `assess/{code}.json`.
  * In `analyze.py`, `cohort(c)` sums only `worker_usage["additional_tokens"]`. Incurred pipeline costs (successor Flash calls and reviewer Luna calls) are omitted from each cohort's token total, biasing $r_P$ and $r_F$ whenever cross-family review costs diverge.
* **Minimal Remedy**:
  In `cmd_item()`, collect token usage for `work-{code}`, `succ-{code}`, and `review-{code}`, storing a summed `total_additional_tokens` alongside the breakdown in `assess/{code}.json`. In `check_budget()` and `analyze.py`, evaluate the 25k cap and cohort token sums against the composite item tokens.

---

### Blocker 2: Coercion of Reviewer Truth Values Bypasses Boolean Type Invariant

* **Exact Code Anchor**:
  `analyze.py#L423-L424`:
  ```python
  ck = {k: bool(v.get("value")) if isinstance(v, dict) else bool(v) for k, v in a["review"]["checks"].items()}
  ```
* **Violated Requirement**:
  Approved handoff §4 step 3 and calibration standards require reviewer decisions to be typed JSON booleans (`True` / `False`), as checked in calibration (`run_study.py#L252-L253`: `type(a) is not bool or type(b) is not bool: raise ValueError`).
* **Mechanism**:
  In Python, `bool("false")`, `bool("null")`, and `bool("0")` evaluate to `True`. If an LLM reviewer outputs stringified values (e.g. `{"value": "false"}`), `is_spo()` coerces failed checks to `True`, converting failing outputs into Substantive Preserved Outputs (SPOs).
* **Minimal Remedy**:
  Enforce explicit boolean matching:
  ```python
  def _to_bool(v):
      val = v.get("value") if isinstance(v, dict) else v
      return val is True

  ck = {k: _to_bool(v) for k, v in a["review"]["checks"].items()}
  ```

---

### Blocker 3: Blinding Breach During Declarer Dispatch (`cwd` Omission)

* **Exact Code Anchor**:
  `run_study.py#L311-L313`:
  ```python
  for a in T["declarers"]:
      t0 = time.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ", time.gmtime())
      r = call(a, text, P.RATE_INSTRUCTION, "declaration", f"declare-{a}")
  ```
* **Violated Requirement**:
  Handoff §4 step 6, §6, and `attestation.json` guarantee: *"declarers run in the EMPTY neutral directory so they cannot see priority rankings; declarations/attestation.json records this"*.
* **Mechanism**:
  While `neutral_check()` verifies that `/private/tmp/study060/neutral` exists, `call()` in `cmd_declare()` does not pass `cwd=NEUTRAL`. The declarer CLI sessions run in the repository directory, where `SessionStart` hooks expose backlog metadata, formula priorities, and mission rankings directly to the declarers.
* **Minimal Remedy**:
  Pass `cwd=NEUTRAL` explicitly:
  ```python
  r = call(a, text, P.RATE_INSTRUCTION, "declaration", f"declare-{a}", cwd=NEUTRAL)
  ```

---

### Blocker 4: Unvalidated Declarer Outputs Cause Silent Dropout in Selection

* **Exact Code Anchor**:
  * `run_study.py#L314-L321`
  * `choose.py#L563-L565`:
    ```python
    if proposer.get(cid) == a or cid not in rows:
        continue
    ```
* **Violated Requirement**:
  Selection protocol requires every candidate in `pool.json` to be rated by every declarer (excluding an agent's own submitted ideas).
* **Mechanism**:
  `cmd_declare()` checks integer bounds on returned rows but does not assert that all expected candidate IDs are present. If an agent truncates or omits cards, `choose.py` silently drops the item (`cid not in rows`). The omitted item receives 0 percentile points and fewer ratings, distorting the rank-sum interest score without failing fast.
* **Minimal Remedy**:
  In `cmd_declare()`, assert complete candidate coverage before serializing declarations:
  ```python
  expected = {c["id"] for c in pool if c.get("proposed_by") != a}
  received = {r["id"] for r in rows}
  missing = expected - received
  if missing:
      raise SystemExit(f"STOP: Declarer {a} omitted items: {missing}")
  ```

---

### Blocker 5: Indeterminate State Logic Flaw in Verdict Decision Table

* **Exact Code Anchor**:
  `analyze.py#L486-L494`:
  ```python
  if not all(gates.values()):
      verdict = "UNASSESSED"
      why = [k for k, v in gates.items() if not v]
  elif B["B1"]["met"] is False or not B["B2"]["met"] or A.startswith("FALSIFIED"):
      verdict, why = "FALSIFIED", ...
  elif A.startswith("UNDECIDED") or A == "not run":
      verdict, why = "UNASSESSED", ["claim A undecided or not run"]
  else:
      verdict, why = "CORROBORATED", []
  ```
* **Violated Requirement**:
  Handoff §4 step 7 and §7: Verdict must be `CORROBORATED` only when both Claim A and Claim B (B1, B2, B3) are positively corroborated; unresolved or unverified metrics must resolve to `UNASSESSED`, never fall through.
* **Mechanism**:
  * If validity gates pass, but `B["B1"]["met"]` is `None` (e.g., edge evaluation path), `B["B1"]["met"] is False` evaluates to `False`. The check skips `FALSIFIED` and falls through to `CORROBORATED`.
  * For `B2`, `not B["B2"]["met"]` treats `None` (indeterminate usage) as `True`, improperly falsifying instead of classifying as `UNASSESSED`.
* **Minimal Remedy**:
  Structure the verdict ladder with explicit positive conditions for corroboration:
  ```python
  if not all(gates.values()):
      verdict, why = "UNASSESSED", [k for k, v in gates.items() if not v]
  elif B["B1"]["met"] is False or B["B2"]["met"] is False or A.startswith("FALSIFIED"):
      verdict, why = "FALSIFIED", [k for k, v in [("B1", B["B1"]["met"]), ("B2", B["B2"]["met"])] if v is False] + (["A"] if A.startswith("FALSIFIED") else [])
  elif B["B1"]["met"] is True and B["B2"]["met"] is True and A.startswith("CORROBORATED"):
      verdict, why = "CORROBORATED", []
  else:
      verdict, why = "UNASSESSED", ["indeterminable or incomplete claim results"]
  ```

### Blocker 6: Unhandled Review Structure Failures Crash Analysis

* **Exact Code Anchor**:
  `run_study.py#L370-L380` and `analyze.py#L423`:
  ```python
  ck = {k: bool(v.get("value")) if isinstance(v, dict) else bool(v) for k, v in a["review"]["checks"].items()}
  ```
* **Violated Requirement**:
  Audit integrity and robust evidence handling: Malformed model outputs must trigger explicit containment or invalid-evidence flags rather than unhandled Python runtime crashes during analysis.
* **Mechanism**:

* **Minimal Remedy**:
  In `cmd_item()`, validate that `isinstance(review, dict)` and `"checks" in review` before persisting; in `analyze.py`, use defensive access `a.get("review", {}).get("checks")` and report malformed assessments as unverified outputs.

### 2.1 Free-tree generation (`generate_free_trees`)

- **Completeness holds.** Every tree on n ≥ 3 vertices has a leaf, and deleting it gives a tree isomorphic to some stored representative on n−1 vertices. Attaching a leaf at every vertex of every representative therefore reaches every isomorphism class.
- **Dedup is sound.** The AHU certificate rooted at the center (or at the bicenter, ordered as a min/max pair) is a complete invariant for free trees. The `[…]` and `(…)` prefixes prevent unicentral/bicentral collisions, and the balanced-paren encoding is uniquely parseable.
- The OEIS match for n = 4..11 is therefore credible.

**Defect E1: the Prüfer "Cayley bijection" check is tautological.**

- **Fix:** test the orbit–stabilizer identity Σ_classes n!/|Aut(T)| = n^{n−2}, or check that per-class labeled counts match n!/|Aut|.
- The README label "Cayley Bijection" overstates what the check does.

**Prüfer decoder correctness:** decoding is correct. The current x always has deg ≥ 2 when its leaf is chosen, and used leaves drop to deg 0.

- **Minor:** the key is recomputed for each pair at O(n log n) string cost. That is fine at this scale.

## 1. Definitions & Mathematical Model

Let $G = (V, E)$ be a simple, connected, undirected, unweighted graph on $n = |V|$ vertices with $m = |E|$ edges and degrees $d_v = \deg_G(v)$.
The simple random walk on $G$ has transition probabilities $P_{u,v} = A_{u,v} / d_u$ and unique stationary distribution $\pi_v = d_v / (2m)$.

**Kemeny's constant** $K(G)$ is defined as the expected hitting time from any starting vertex $i \in V$ to a target vertex $j$ drawn from $\pi$:
$$K(G) = \sum_{j \in V \setminus \{i\}} \pi_j m_{i,j}$$
where $m_{i,j}$ is the mean first passage time from $i$ to $j$.

For any non-isomorphic free tree $T$ on $n$ vertices ($m = n-1$) and any missing edge $e = \{u, v\} \notin E(T)$ (so tree distance $d_T(u, v) \ge 2$), adding $e$ produces the unicyclic graph $T + e$ on $n$ vertices and $n$ edges containing a unique cycle of length $L = d_T(u, v) + 1$.

The change in Kemeny's constant is:
$$\Delta K(T, e) = K(T + e) - K(T)$$
A pair $(T, e)$ exhibits **random-walk Braess's paradox** if and only if:
$$\Delta K(T, e) > \varepsilon, \quad \varepsilon = 10^{-9}$$

## 2. Mathematical Background & Tension

For a connected, undirected, unweighted graph $G = (V, E)$ on $n$ vertices with $m = |E|$ edges, a simple random walk transitions from vertex $u$ to a uniformly chosen neighbor $v \sim u$ with probability $P_{u,v} = 1/d_u$. Its unique stationary distribution is $\pi_v = \frac{d_v}{2m}$.

**Kemeny's constant** $K(G)$ is the expected number of steps to reach a randomly chosen target vertex $j \sim \pi$ starting from $i$:
$$K(G) = \sum_{j \neq i} \pi_j m_{i,j}$$
Remarkably (Kemeny, 1960), this sum is **independent of the starting vertex $i$** and equals both:
1. **Fundamental-matrix trace**: $K_{\text{hit}}(G) = \operatorname{Tr}\!\left((I - P + \mathbf{1}\pi^T)^{-1}\right) - 1$, where $m_{i,j} = (Z_{j,j} - Z_{i,j})/\pi_j$.
2. **Spectral sum**: $K_{\text{spec}}(G) = \sum_{k=2}^n \frac{1}{1 - \lambda_k(P)}$, where $1 = \lambda_1 > \lambda_2 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n$ are the eigenvalues of $P = D^{-1}A$ (equivalently of the symmetric matrix $S = D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2}$).

By Chandra et al. (1996) and Tetali (1991), commute times satisfy $C(u,v) = m_{u,v} + m_{v,u} = 2m R_{\text{eff}}(u,v)$, which gives the electrical-network representation:
$$K(G) = m \sum_{x \in V} \sum_{y \in V} \pi_x \pi_y R_{\text{eff}}(x,y) = \frac{1}{4m} \sum_{x,y \in V} d_x d_y R_{\text{eff}}(x,y)$$

When we add a single missing edge $e = \{u,v\} \notin E$ to a tree $T$ ($m = n-1 \to n$):
- **Rayleigh Monotonicity (Speedup force)**: Every pairwise effective resistance $R_{\text{eff}}(x,y)$ along pathways using the new cycle decreases or stays unchanged; specifically, for vertices on the cycle of length $L = d_T(u,v) + 1$, resistances drop by $\Delta R$.
- **Stationary Shift & Edge Dilution (Slowdown force)**: Total edges increase from $n-1$ to $n$, and degrees $d_u, d_v$ each increase by $1$, shifting stationary weight toward $\{u,v\}$. If $e = \{u,v\}$ connects two vertices at short distance (especially $d_T(u,v) = 2$, forming a triangle), the resistance reduction is tiny ($\Delta R_{\text{eff}}(u,v) = 2 - 2/3 = 4/3$ locally, saving only one hop), while the extra edge traps random-walk transitions inside the triangle and increases the expected time to reach distant leaves!

Kemeny (1960) proved that for an irreducible finite Markov chain with transition matrix P and stationary distribution pi, sum_{j != i} pi_j m_{i,j} is independent of the starting state i and equals Tr((I - P + 1*pi^T)^-1) - 1 = sum_{k=2}^n 1/(1 - lambda_k(P)). Tetali (1991) and Chandra et al. (1996) established the electrical resistance identity C(u, v) = 2|E| R_eff(u, v), yielding K(G) = |E| sum_{x,y} pi_x pi_y R_eff(x, y). Prior spectral graph theory literature on Braess's paradox for Kemeny's constant (unverified background context, not inspected or relied on as evidence here) shows that adding an edge can increase K(G) in specific families, but the exact prevalence across all non-isomorphic trees on n = 7..11, its monotonicity with n, and the quantitative share at distance d_T(u, v) = 2 versus diameter-endpoint shortcuts had not been enumerated in this repository.

## Target
Spectral graph theory and finite Markov chains: Kemeny's constant under single-edge additions across all non-isomorphic trees on n = 4..11 vertices (exact enumeration in zero-dependency Python standard library; bounded local CPU)

## Lessons learned
- For n in {7..11}, all 2,340 observed random-walk Braess paradoxes in trees occurred at shortcut distances d_T(u,v) in {2, 3, 4} (87.65% at d=2, 11.75% at d=3, 0.60% at d=4, and 0 at d>=5), with the d=2 share declining from 100.00% at n=7 to 85.50% at n=11; whether d>=5 paradoxes emerge at n>=12 remains open.
- Across n in {7..11}, the raw missing-edge paradox fraction p(n) fell monotonically (20.00% to 13.83%) even as the maximum slowdown Delta_K rose (+1.2619 to +3.4939), whereas the automorphism-orbit-deduplicated paradox fraction stayed nearly flat (11.39% to 13.30%), showing that raw edge-pair prevalence is sensitive to automorphism multiplicity.
- Diameter-endpoint shortcuts are not immune to Braess's paradox when the tree diameter itself is small (145/1,746 diameter shortcuts increased K(T), all at diam(T) <= 4); for n <= 11, no shortcut at distance d_T(u,v) >= 5 increased K(T).

## 1. Motivation and Origin
In `MISSION-063`, empirical testing across $16,355$ tree shortcut edge additions demonstrated that adding edges can degrade global mixing times (Kemeny's constant $K(G)$) on random-walk topologies—falsifying intuitive monotonicity and diameter-endpoint immunity. The transfer reflection raised the question of whether adding optional coordination or routing connections in agent workflows could similarly improve a local metric (such as estimated critical path length or stage latency) while degrading end-to-end delivery metrics (cost, makespan, contention, or failure cascade rates).

This observation serves as conceptual motivation and a falsifiable hypothesis source—not empirical evidence about orchestration systems.

---

## 2. Mandatory Distinction: Representation in `orchestrating-agent-work`
The companion orchestration skill (`../agent-plugins-skills/plugins/agent-orchestration/.apm/skills/orchestrating-agent-work`) and its DAG runner (`scripts/graph_runner.py`) represent specific edge types:
1. **Mandatory precedence/dependency edges (`dependencies`)**: Explicit topological ordering required for data availability and correctness (e.g. `parallel_read` $\to$ `sync_barrier`, or strict total ordering between `sequential_mutation` nodes). Removing required dependencies, authorization gates, validation scripts, or human approval barriers to optimize a score is strictly forbidden by topology rules and constitution.
2. **Optional routing or delegation alternatives (`fallback_node_id`, dynamic routing)**: Edges that provide an alternative execution path when a primary node fails.
3. **Feedback/retry transitions (`max_retries_per_node`)**: In-node reset and retry cycles before triggering a fallback.
4. **Knowledge/context links (`input_bindings`, scratch directory sharing)**: Declarative data passing through `$GRAPH_SCRATCH_DIR`.

---

## 3. Two-Stage Research Design

### Stage A: Establish Applicability
Inspect companion source references, runner state machine (`graph_runner.py`), and test suites (`tests/test_graph_runner.py`, `tests/test_loop_strategies.py`). Identify which specific transformation is genuinely supported by the execution model:
- e.g., adding an optional speculative parallel read, eager verification bypass, or direct dependency shortcut across barriers.
- Document actual scheduling/concurrency behavior, supported edge semantics, and existing safeguards.
- *Negative Gate*: If no relevant edge transformation exists within the genuine execution model, report the analogy as inapplicable rather than manufacturing an artificial scheduler.

### Stage B: Test One Applicable Transformation
Before held-out execution:
- Specify the exact edge type and graph transformation.
- Define the local benefit intended (e.g., reduction in planned critical path latency or barrier delay).
- Establish matched baseline and variant workflow fixtures with identical deliverable requirements.
- Define deterministic task durations, simulated failure schedules, and resource contention.
- Measure end-to-end outcomes: delivery acceptance, total work/cost, makespan, retries, and wasted computation.
- Evaluate against frozen acceptance criteria on held-out fixtures.

---

## 4. Candidate Falsifiable Hypothesis
> "Among at least 24 frozen matched workflow fixtures, adding the selected optional planning edge improves the declared local metric but worsens at least one predeclared end-to-end cost metric by 10% or more in at least 20% of fixtures, without changing task requirements."

# Network Connectivity and Neural Information Flow

**Status:** KEEP  
**Date:** 2026-11-08  
**Topic:** Relationship between graph connectivity, rewiring interventions, random-walk metrics, and neural message-passing bottlenecks.  
**Related Missions:** [`MISSION-063`](../../missions/MISSION-063.json) (motivating inquiry), [`MISSION-064`](../../missions/MISSION-064.json) (proposed follow-up on agent workflow DAG execution).

---

## 1. Research Question

> **When do added edges or changed connection weights help or harm information propagation, and can random-walk measures predict the effect?**

In graph-structured computation and neural representation learning, adding edges ("shortcuts" or "rewiring") is frequently attempted to shorten path lengths between distant nodes. However, both discrete spectral graph theory and empirical graph neural network (GNN) evaluations reveal non-monotonic trade-offs: local additions can distort stationary distributions, alter curvature bottlenecks, increase over-squashing, or accelerate oversmoothing. This dossier synthesizes relevant literature to analyze when connectivity changes help versus harm information flow.

---

## 2. Bibliographic Survey and Verified Source Findings

*Note: All literature summaries below are based on inspection of published arXiv titles, author declarations, and official abstracts.*

### Source 1: Di Giovanni et al. (2023)
- **Title:** *On Over-Squashing in Message Passing Neural Networks: The Impact of Width, Depth, and Topology*
- **Authors:** Francesco Di Giovanni, Lorenzo Giusti, Federico Barbero, Giulia Luise, Pietro Liò, Michael M. Bronstein
- **ArXiv:** [arXiv:2302.02941](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.02941)
- **Inspection Basis:** Abstract inspection.
- **Reported Findings:**
  1. **Width vs. Depth Trade-off:** Neural network width can mitigate over-squashing, but increases overall model sensitivity. Conversely, increasing depth fails to mitigate over-squashing, as deeper layers become dominated by vanishing gradients.
  2. **Role of Topology & Commute Time:** Graph topology plays the dominant role in over-squashing: over-squashing is mathematically proven to concentrate between node pairs with **high commute (access) time**.
  3. **Rewiring Grounding:** Provides a theoretical framework justifying graph rewiring methods that reduce pairwise commute/access times.

### Source 2: Saber & Salehi-Abari (2024/2025)
- **Title:** *Over-Squashing in GNNs and Causal Inference of Rewiring Strategies*
- **Authors:** Danial Saber, Amirali Salehi-Abari
- **ArXiv:** [arXiv:2508.09265](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.09265)
- **Inspection Basis:** Abstract inspection.
- **Reported Findings:**
  1. **Causal Quantification of Rewiring:** Measures pairwise over-squashing via mutual sensitivity decay rates and defines graph-level metrics (prevalence, intensity, variability, extremity).
  2. **Non-Uniform Benefits:** Graph-classification datasets suffer significantly from over-squashing, where restrained rewiring helps performance; however, in node-classification benchmarks, rewiring often *increases* over-squashing, and downstream performance variations are uncorrelated with over-squashing changes.
  3. **Harm of Over-Rewiring:** Aggressive rewiring or rewiring applied to minimally over-squashed graphs fails to help and can actively harm model performance.

### Source 3: Wu, Ajorlou, Wu, & Jadbabaie (2023)
- **Title:** *Demystifying Oversmoothing in Attention-Based Graph Neural Networks*
- **Authors:** Xinyi Wu, Amir Ajorlou, Zihui Wu, Ali Jadbabaie
- **ArXiv:** [arXiv:2305.16102](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16102)
- **Inspection Basis:** Abstract inspection.
- **Reported Findings:**
  1. **Attention Mechanisms Do Not Prevent Oversmoothing:** Formulates attention-based GNNs as nonlinear time-varying dynamical systems using products of inhomogeneous matrices and joint spectral radius.
  2. **Exponential Loss of Expressive Power:** Proves that graph attention mechanisms (GATs, graph transformers) still lose expressive power exponentially with depth, despite asymmetric, state-dependent, and time-varying aggregation weights.
  3. **Broad Generalization:** Extends oversmoothing bounds from symmetric Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) to asymmetric, random-walk GCNs and transformers under standard activation functions (ReLU, GELU, SiLU).

### Source 4: Topping et al. (2021/2022)
- **Title:** *Understanding Over-Squashing and Bottlenecks on Graphs via Curvature*
- **Authors:** Jake Topping, Francesco Di Giovanni, Benjamin Paul Chamberlain, Xiaowen Dong, Michael M. Bronstein
- **ArXiv:** [arXiv:2111.14522](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.14522)
- **Inspection Basis:** Abstract inspection.
- **Reported Findings:**
  1. **Curvature Bottlenecks:** Analyzes graph bottlenecks causing information distortion where $k$-hop neighborhoods grow exponentially.
  2. **Negatively Curved Edges:** Introduces an edge-based combinatorial Ricci curvature and proves that negatively curved edges are responsible for over-squashing bottlenecks.
  3. **Curvature Rewiring:** Formulates targeted curvature-based rewiring (adding edges across negatively curved bottlenecks or removing bridge edges) to mitigate over-squashing.

## 4. Key Limitations

1. **Distinct Formal Quantities:**
   - **Kemeny's Constant ($K(G)$)**: $\sum_j \pi_j m_{ij}$, an intrinsic spectral invariant of the random walk measuring expected steps to reach a $\pi$-distributed destination from any starting node.
   - **Commute Time ($C(u,v) = m_{uv} + m_{vu}$)**: The round-trip expected time between a specific pair of nodes (proportional to effective resistance $2m R_{\text{eff}}(u,v)$).
   - **Over-Squashing**: Decay of the Jacobian sensitivity $\left|\frac{\partial h_u^{(L)}}{\partial x_v}\right|$ as a function of path length, layer depth $L$, and neighborhood growth.
   - **Oversmoothing**: Dirichlet energy collapse $\frac{1}{|V|} \sum_{u} \|h_u - \bar{h}\|^2 \to 0$ where node representations become indistinguishable across depth.
   - **Downstream Accuracy**: Task-specific loss on node or graph classification benchmarks.
2. **No Model Training in MISSION-063:** MISSION-063 investigated discrete linear algebra (fundamental matrices, Laplacian pseudoinverses, Jacobi eigensystems) on undirected trees. It did not train any machine learning weights or compute neural loss functions.
3. **Different Intervention Classes:** Adding an unweighted edge to an adjacency matrix $A$ alters graph topology and degree distributions. In contrast, message-passing reweighting adjusts normalization matrices, and neural weight optimization updates parameter tensors $W \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$. These interventions operate on different mathematical structures.
4. **No Universal Claim:** No general law or universal predictive relationship is claimed between Kemeny's constant and deep learning dynamics.

# MISSION-066: Equal-temperament records for 5-limit harmony

**Verdict: CORROBORATED** (gate passed; H1 and H2 held). Freeze commit `8041b5b8b`; `freeze.json` hashes protocol.md and evaluate_et.py.

## Question
If the octave is split into N equal steps, how well can it play the just fifth (3/2), major third (5/4) and minor third (6/5)? Measure: the worst of the three errors in cents, each interval rounded to its nearest step. A division is a *record* if it beats every smaller division.

## Results (`results.json`, `dev_results.json`)
| N | worst error (cents) | fifth | major third | minor third |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 12 | 15.64 | -1.96 | +13.69 | -15.64 |
| 19 | 7.37 | | | |
| 31 | 5.96 | -5.18 | +0.78 | -5.96 |
| 34 | 3.93 | +3.93 | +1.92 | +2.01 |
| 53 | 1.41 | -0.07 | -1.41 | +1.34 |
| 118 | 0.39 | -0.26 | +0.13 | -0.39 |
| 171 | 0.35 | -0.20 | -0.35 | +0.15 |

Full record list for N 1..200: 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 12, 19, 31, 34, 53, 118, 171.

## Observations
- The textbook list is right under this measure: 12, 19, 31, 34, 53 and 118 are all records.
- Nothing between 54 and 117 beats 53. Of my allowed set, 65 and 87 never became records.
- 12-TET's weakness is the thirds, not the fifth: its fifth is 2 cents off, but its thirds are 14-16 cents off.
- In units of its own step, 118 (0.038 step) is better than 171 (0.050 step). 171 wins only in absolute cents.

## Limitations
- H2 was a superset prediction (7 allowed values), so it was a weaker test than H1. Its main risk was an unexpected record such as 41, 72 or 99, and none appeared.
- Each interval is rounded on its own (patent rounding), so for some N the thirds and the fifth are not mutually consistent. A consistency-based or weighted measure (for example Tenney-Euclidean) could give a different list. I did not test this.
- 7-limit intervals (7/4) and N > 200 are out of scope.
- No independent model review was run, because the computation is short, deterministic and checked by the gate.

# MISSION-067: Random change ringing as a shuffle

**Verdict: FALSIFIED** (gate passed; H1 held, H2 failed). Freeze commit `abda842f3` hashes protocol.md, evaluate_ringing.py and discovery.md. Discovery provenance is in `discovery.md`.

## Question
In change ringing each bell moves at most one place per row, so a change is a set of disjoint neighbour swaps. If a band rang *random* changes, how fast would the bells become well mixed, compared with the classic slow shuffle that swaps one random neighbouring pair at a time (lazy)? Does parallelism save work, or only time?

## Result (exact, `results.json`, `dev_results.json`; TV <= 0.25 from rounds)
| n | t_C (changes) | t_A (lazy steps) | speedup R | swaps C | swaps A | C/A swaps |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 5 | 11 | 2.20 | 6.3 | 5.5 | 1.14 |
| 5 | 10 | 25 | 2.50 | 14.3 | 12.5 | 1.14 |
| 6 | 17 | 49 | 2.88 | 28.3 | 24.5 | 1.16 |
| 7 | 24 | 85 | 3.54 | 45.6 | 42.5 | 1.07 |
| 8 | 34 | 135 | 3.97 | 73.2 | 67.5 | 1.08 |

- **H1 held**: the time speedup grows with n (2.88, then 3.54, then 3.97).
- **H2 failed**: random changes use 7-16% *more* total swaps than one-at-a-time swapping. Ringing's parallelism buys time, not work. The speedup roughly tracks swaps per step (s_C = 1.67, 1.90, 2.15 against the baseline's 0.5 per step).

## Surprise
The swap overhead fell from 1.16 (n=6) to 1.07-1.08 (n=7,8). With only two held-out sizes and integer mixing times, I cannot tell whether it tends to 1 or stays above it.

## Limitations
- Exact for n <= 8 only, with no asymptotic claim. Mixing times are integers, so ratios carry granularity error of about 1/t.
- The random chain borrows ringing's move set but not its rules: real ringing forbids repeated rows and uses methods, not chance.
- The comparison is asymmetric by design: chain A is lazy (otherwise periodic), chain C is not.
- No independent model review: the computation is deterministic and gate-checked, and headroom was limited (claude ~33%). The literature on parallel adjacent-swap shuffles was not checked, so this is "new here" only.

## Association assessment
The association was **generative**: ringing's one-place rule plus bee-style parallel recruitment produced the time-vs-work question. It was not tested as a transfer that improves anything. The ringing-to-shuffle analogy breaks at the no-repeat rule (see discovery.md).

## Reproduce
`python3 evaluate_ringing.py --mode heldout` (stdlib, ~5 s CPU).

# MISSION-067 discovery note (associative exploration, pre-registration)

Selection method: **deliberate diverse selection** (not random; no sampler used). No domain ledger exists; provenance is kept here.

## Domains
1. **English change ringing** (history/physical practice). Phenomenon: church bells rung in permuted orders ("rows"). Constraint: a heavy bell swings through a full circle each stroke, so between consecutive rows each bell can move at most one place. A "change" is therefore a set of disjoint swaps of adjacent bells. Tension: ringers prize *extents* (every row exactly once), a deterministic, exhaustive walk, never randomness.
2. **Card shuffling / Markov chain mixing** (mathematics). Mechanism: repeated random moves drive a deck toward uniform; mixing time depends on what moves are allowed. Known (from memory, unverified here): random adjacent transpositions mix slowly, on the order of n^3 log n steps.
3. **Braided rivers** (geomorphology). Channels split and rejoin; sediment moves only locally, but the braid pattern rearranges globally. Uncertain: how fast local exchange produces global reordering.
4. **Honeybee waggle-dance recruitment** (biology). Many local, parallel signals at once rather than one global broadcast. Uncertain mapping to anything permutational.

## Crossings (short)
- Ringing x shuffling: *a change is a parallel adjacent-swap shuffle*. If a band rang changes at random instead of by method, how many changes until the order is "well mixed"? **(developed)**
- Ringing x rivers: bells drift one place per row like sediment one bar per flood; descendant: "hunting" bells (moving steadily one place per row) resemble a channel migrating. Kept as provenance only.
- Shuffling x bees: parallel local moves vs one global move. Descendant, combined with ringing: does parallelism *save work* (total swaps), or only *time* (number of changes)? **(this became H2)**
- Rivers x shuffling (awkward idea, developed fairly): braided channels as a sorting network. Shared vocabulary ("exchange") but no clear stochastic model; dismissed for now, with no claim made.
- Deceptive similarity: ringing forbids repeating a row, but random shuffles repeat freely. So the random-change chain is *not* ringing; it only borrows the ringing move set. Recorded as a limitation.

## Candidate briefs
1. **Random-change shuffle mixing** (ringing + shuffling + bee parallelism). Exactly computable on S_n for n <= 8 with stdlib. Interest: does the physical "one place per row" rule still allow fast mixing once many swaps happen in parallel? Risk: per-step speedup may be trivial (it does more swaps). That is why H2 counts swaps. **Selected.**
2. Do classic methods (Plain Bob) produce row sequences that pass randomness tests? Rejected: an extent is deterministic and the test choice dominates the answer.
3. Braided-river sorting network. Rejected: no defensible model in this session.

## Hypothesis
Provisional: explicit cross-record and transition checks reduce invalid transitions accepted by the current baseline (A: installed scripts and validators) without materially blocking valid work. A specialized semantic implementation (C: SHACL or a solver) adds value only if it improves coverage, clarity or maintenance over equivalent ordinary-code checks (B), with policy requirements and available evidence held equivalent across B and C. Numeric thresholds and case counts are not yet defined; they are set after the inventory and development phase and frozen before held-out execution.

## Falsification criteria
Not yet frozen. To be specified with numeric thresholds after the inventory/development phase and before held-out execution. In outline: the hypothesis fails if B and C accept no fewer held-out invalid transitions than A, or block valid transitions materially more often; C's added value fails if it does not exceed B on coverage, clarity or maintenance at equal rules and evidence. Rules must not be derived from held-out failures. Acceptable outcomes include: existing enforcement sufficient; small script improvements sufficient; semantic validator adds measurable value; evidence insufficient.

## Experiment / method
1) Inventory existing enforcement: map each relevant invariant to the code that enforces it; examine Agentic OS capabilities; separate missing from bypassable checks. 2) Define a small domain model (candidates: Mission, Attempt, Evidence, Verdict, Authorization, Lease, SourceRevision, Export, RemoteReceipt), only the relationships the selected cases need, marking trusted observations vs agent assertions. 3) Compare A (current scripts), B (minimal ordinary-code preconditions/transition checks) and C (one semantic implementation, SHACL or solver, only if research shows a fit) on identical cases. 4) Use confirmed historical failures plus valid and already-fixed counterparts as development examples. 5) Freeze a bounded evaluation (invalid/valid transitions, stale/missing evidence, interruption/resume, duplicate requests, concurrent change between validation and execution; rejection before side effect) and run held-out cases on isolated fixtures with simulated publication.

# Explicit Semantic and Lifecycle Contracts for Agent Reliability

**Status:** KEEP  
**Date:** 2026-11-08  
**Topic:** Whether a small, explicit model of entities, relationships and permitted state transitions prevents agent errors that Sanctuary's current schemas, scripts and operating instructions do not already prevent.  
**Related Missions:** [`MISSION-068`](../../missions/MISSION-068.json) (motivating PROPOSED mission; not executed), [`MISSION-036`](../../missions/MISSION-036.json) (evidence and verdict contracts), [`MISSION-038`](../../missions/MISSION-038.json) (lease fencing and idempotent transitions).

---

## 1. Origin and attribution

- **Question:** proposed by Richard (human partner) after Frank Coyle's talk *Why Agentic Systems Need Ontologies* (<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Sir59K8ZDPU>).
- **Inspection of the talk:** its indexed description and chapter list only, not a full transcript. No claim here rests on the talk's detailed content.
- **Comparative research design:** proposed by ChatGPT (OpenAI). Recorded and registered by claude-code (Anthropic) on 2026-11-08, with the design preserved as given.

## 2. Research question

> Does a small, explicit model of entities, relationships and permitted state transitions prevent errors that Sanctuary's current schemas, scripts and operating instructions do not already prevent? If it does, does a specialized semantic implementation (SHACL, OWL or a solver) add value over equivalent ordinary-code checks?

This is a research question. It does **not** assume that RDF, OWL, SHACL, Z3, a knowledge graph or a new control plane must be adopted.

## 3. Sources (reading depth: abstracts and introductory material only)

ChatGPT inspected the paper abstracts and the standards' introductory material. Nothing below reflects a full-text methodological review; that review belongs to mission execution, before the experimental protocol is finalized.

1. **W3C OWL 2 Web Ontology Language Primer**: <https://www.w3.org/TR/owl2-primer/>. Relevance: a vocabulary for entities (classes, individuals), relationships (properties) and logical inference over them. Open question: whether open-world inference fits closed, operational lifecycle checks at all.
2. **W3C Shapes Constraint Language (SHACL)**: <https://www.w3.org/TR/shacl/>. Relevance: validation of graph data against explicit constraints ("shapes"). This is the closest standard analogue to cross-record validation of manifests, leases, exports and receipts.
3. **Solver-Aided Verification of Policy Compliance in Tool-Augmented LLM Agents**: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.20449>. Relevance: runtime interception of proposed tool calls, with Z3 checks over observable state and arguments. The authors report fewer policy violations while maintaining task accuracy (author-reported; not independently checked here).
4. **Verification-Aware Planning for Multi-Agent Systems (VeriMAP)**: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.17109>. Relevance: planner-defined verification functions for each subtask, covering dependencies, acceptance criteria and handoffs.

## 4. Proposed research sequence (for later execution; not started)

1. **Inventory existing enforcement.** Inspect the current mission schema, coordination, lifecycle, preservation, authorization and shared orchestration capabilities. Map each relevant invariant to the code that already enforces it. Examine related Agentic OS capabilities before proposing new machinery. Distinguish missing checks from checks that exist but can be bypassed.
2. **Define a small domain model.** Candidate entities: Mission, Attempt, Evidence, Verdict, Authorization, Lease, SourceRevision, Export, RemoteReceipt. Define only the relationships needed by the selected failure cases. Identify which facts come from trusted system observations and which are only agent assertions.
3. **Compare three approaches on identical cases:**
   - A. Current installed scripts and validators.
   - B. Minimal ordinary-code preconditions and state-transition checks.
   - C. Explicit semantic contracts using SHACL or a solver, if research shows a useful fit. Select one implementation, not every stack.

   Keep policy requirements and available evidence equivalent across B and C; otherwise extra rules could be mistaken for a benefit of the technology.
4. **Historical failures as development examples** (to be confirmed from repository records; do not assume they remain unfixed; include valid counterparts and already-fixed cases):
   - Startup unexpectedly initiating preservation writes.
   - Lease updates resetting a resolved mission to IN_PROGRESS.
   - Declaring delivery complete before required publication or preservation.
   - Confusing an unassessed experiment with a falsified hypothesis.
   - Treating a receipt for an older revision as proof of current persistence.
5. **Freeze a bounded evaluation before held-out cases.** Include invalid and valid transitions, stale or missing evidence, interruption and resume, duplicate requests, and a concurrent state change between validation and execution. Test whether rejection occurs *before* the prohibited side effect. Use isolated fixtures and simulated publication, never live destructive operations or remote writes.

## 5. Provisional hypothesis and measures

**Hypothesis (provisional):** explicit cross-record and transition checks reduce the invalid transitions accepted by the current baseline without materially blocking valid work. A specialized semantic implementation adds value only if it improves coverage, clarity or maintenance over equivalent ordinary-code checks.

**Measures:**
- Invalid transitions accepted.
- Valid transitions incorrectly blocked.
- Failures prevented before side effects.
- Correct handling of stale, unknown and conflicting evidence.
- Implementation and maintenance effort, dependencies and runtime overhead.
- Model tokens, only if a separately justified, bounded live-agent test is run.

## 6. Experimental discipline and limits

- Numeric thresholds, case counts and budgets are specified after the inventory and development phase, then frozen before held-out execution.
- Rules are never derived from held-out failures.
- A deterministic fixture study cannot establish improved real-agent behaviour.
- A logically consistent assertion is not necessarily factually true.
- An ontology does not provide transactional locking, authorization or idempotency merely by describing those concepts.

**Acceptable outcomes:** existing enforcement is sufficient; small improvements to existing scripts are sufficient; a semantic validator provides measurable additional value; or the evidence is insufficient, with limitations recorded and no adoption forced.

## 7. Relation to existing missions

- **MISSION-036** (Preregistered Evidence Contracts) tests contract fields for claims and verdicts. Overlaps on "unassessed vs falsified" and evidence validity. It does not compare approaches across the whole lifecycle.
- **MISSION-038** (Crash-Safe Coordination) tests lease fencing and idempotent transitions under faults. Overlaps on concurrency and duplicate requests. It is about coordination mechanics, not a semantic model.
- MISSION-068 is registered separately because neither mission asks the comparative question (baseline vs ordinary-code checks vs semantic contracts).

## 8. Status of this dossier

Registration-time synthesis only. No experiment has been run, no capability implemented, and no source read beyond abstracts and introductions.

# MISSION-023: MLX speculative decoding on an M1 (16 GB)

**Verdict: FALSIFIED.** Speed criterion failed, memory criterion held. Freeze commit `1e43214ab` hashes protocol.md, bench_spec.py and dev_results.json; the selected config was fixed on dev before the held-out run.

## Setup
Target `mlx-community/Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct-4bit`; drafts Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B and 3B (4-bit, MLX); mlx-lm 0.32.2 (`uvx`); greedy decoding, 256 new tokens, chat template. The local MLX server on :8080 was stopped during measurement and restarted afterwards.

## Dev sweep (3 prompts; selects only)
| config | median tok/s | median speedup | peak GiB |
|---|---|---|---|
| baseline | 13.8 | 1.00 | 4.15 |
| 1.5B, k=2 | 19.9 | **1.48** | 4.97 |
| 1.5B, k=4 | 18.2 | 1.36 | 4.97 |
| 3B, k=2 | 15.5 | 1.15 | 5.80 |
| 3B, k=4 | 14.5 | 1.05 | 5.81 |

## Held-out (10 prompts, selected config 1.5B k=2)
- Baseline 14.1 tok/s median; speculative 19.7 tok/s median.
- **Median speedup 1.40x** (min 1.30x), below the 1.6x threshold, so H fails.
- **Peak memory 4.99 GiB**, within the 8 GiB budget.
- 10/10 outputs token-identical to baseline (lossless, as expected for greedy).
- Draft acceptance about 63% of emitted tokens.

## Observations
- The smaller draft wins: the 3B draft has the same acceptance rate as the 1.5B (about 65% at k=2) but costs more per step, so it gives almost no gain.
- Larger k raises acceptance (77% at k=4) but lowers throughput. Rejected drafts waste compute on a bandwidth-limited M1.
- Speedup was very stable across prompts (1.30-1.5x); baseline throughput varied by <2%.

## Limitations
One machine, one run per prompt, short coding/explanation prompts (code-heavy or repetitive text may accept more drafts), no 0.5B draft tested, k only in {2,4}. mlx-lm's generation tok/s excludes prompt processing. The selection of 1 of 4 configs on 3 dev prompts is a small sample.

## Practical takeaway
On this M1, a 1.5B draft with k=2 is a free ~1.4x speed-up with identical greedy output and about +0.8 GiB memory. It is worth enabling for local Qwen generation, but it is not the 1.6x the mission predicted.

## Reproduce
`HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 uvx --from mlx-lm==0.32.2 python bench_spec.py --mode heldout --draft 1.5B --k 2` (MLX server stopped first).

| C3 no inference while idle | 15 s idle: 0 dispatches, 0.01 s CPU (0.07%) |
| C4 failure rail | 3 failures -> BLOCKED_ON_HUMAN; 4th job held; ran after `reset` |
| C5 sequential state changes | order 0,1,2; 3 dispatches; 0 unparseable reads during writes |
| C6 gates | no `authorized_by`, `copilot`, bypass flag, non-isolated without opt-in: all REJECTED, 0 dispatches |
| C7 crash recovery | job group killed on daemon stop, job back to QUEUED, completed on attempt 2 |

Run 1 (frozen design): C1, C3-C7 passed; C2 could not be measured (see protocol).

## Live demo (`evidence/live_demo/`; not part of the verdict)
One daemon pass (`run --once`, 2.5 s wall) ran a real Claude Haiku job through cli-agent (isolated; exit 0; output `SANCTUARY-DAEMON-OK`; usage not reported by the backend) and a shell job that made a verified commit (`require_commit`) in a scratch git repository.

## Findings
- **Code defect found and fixed in dev:** on macOS `killpg(pgid, 0)` raises EPERM when only the zombie group leader is left; reap the leader while waiting.
- **cli-agent gap:** `run_agent.py` adds `--dangerously-skip-permissions` for claude/agy unless `--isolated`. Isolated claude in `-p` mode cannot edit files, so unattended editing currently needs an explicit bypass opt-in. A narrower `--permission-mode acceptEdits` plus allowed-tools option belongs upstream in cli-agent.
- **Unattended auth:** Claude's sign-in warned of expiry within days; long-running use needs `claude setup-token`.
- **Rails interact:** the C2 test failure was the C4 rail working; tests of one rail must isolate it from the others.

## Bootstrap decision
The daemon is started by the human (foreground or launchd), never by session bootstrap: startup must stay observational, and starting a dispatcher is a state-changing act under the Human Gate. A read-only status line in the boot briefing is a possible follow-up.

## Limits
Mechanics only, on one macOS machine; one job at a time; no token-budget rail yet (wall-clock and failure-count only); Linux inotify untested; the demo used one cheap model and a trivial task, so it does not show the reliability of real agent work.

# MISSION-001 protocol: zero-token supervisor daemon (frozen before the confirmatory run)

## Hypothesis (manifest, unchanged)
A zero-token, event-driven supervisor daemon can reliably orchestrate multi-step agent lifecycles, handle sequential state changes, and enforce operational rails (process timeouts, budget trips, state rollback) without burning tokens during idle state monitoring.

## Falsification criteria (manifest) made measurable
The hypothesis is FALSIFIED if, in the confirmatory run of `test_daemon.py --confirm`, any of these fails:

| ID | Criterion | Measure | Pass rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | Detect a queued job within 2 s | wall time from the atomic write of a QUEUED job to the daemon's RUNNING write | all 20 trials < 2.0 s |
| C2 | Hard timeout enforced by SIGKILL | job `sh -c 'sleep 60 & sleep 60; wait'` with `timeout_sec=2` | in all 5 trials: status TIMED_OUT, ended < timeout + 4 s (SIGTERM, 2 s grace, then SIGKILL), and no process of the job's process group is alive afterwards |
| C3 | No model inference while idle | daemon idles 15 s with an empty queue | 0 dispatches, and daemon CPU time < 1% of wall time |
| C4 | Failure rail (budget trip) | 3 consecutive jobs exiting non-zero | 3rd job leaves the daemon in BLOCKED_ON_HUMAN; a 4th QUEUED job is not dispatched until `reset` |
| C5 | Sequential state changes | 3 jobs queued in order | each runs exactly once, in queue order, states QUEUED -> RUNNING -> COMPLETED, no job file ever unparseable mid-run |
| C6 | Authorization and policy gates | job without `authorized_by`; job with `cli: copilot`; job with a forbidden flag | none is dispatched; each ends REJECTED with a reason |

CORROBORATED if all six pass. UNASSESSED if the suite cannot run (environment failure).

## Scope and instruments
- POC location: `LEARNING/experiments/mission-001/daemon/sanctuary_daemon.py` (stdlib only; macOS `select.kqueue` watcher, polling fallback).
- Tests use the `shell` runner with deterministic commands. No model is called by the confirmatory suite.
- The `cli-agent` runner (dispatching through `run_agent.py` with `--cwd/--allowed-root/--claim-dir/--timeout/--result-json`) is exercised once in a separate, labelled live demo in a scratch git repository. The demo is evidence of end-to-end wiring, not part of the verdict.
- Development: the suite is iterated in dev mode (fewer trials) until the instrument is correct; then protocol.md, the daemon and the test file are hash-frozen and committed, and `--confirm` runs once.

## Rollback (state rollback in the hypothesis)
"State rollback" is tested as: a job interrupted by daemon shutdown (SIGTERM) while RUNNING is returned to QUEUED on the next start (recovery), not lost or duplicated. This is criterion C7, assessed in the same suite:

| C7 | Crash recovery | daemon stopped while a job is RUNNING, then restarted | the job's process group is killed on stop; on restart the job is re-queued once (attempt 2) and completes |

## Limits
A deterministic fixture suite shows the daemon's mechanics on this machine. It does not show reliability of real agent work, behaviour under weeks of uptime, or Linux behaviour (inotify not tested). Detection latency is measured on a local APFS disk.

## Budget
Local CPU only for the suite (< 5 min). Live demo: one Claude Haiku dispatch through cli-agent, max 120 s.

## Development disclosures (recorded before the freeze; criteria unchanged)
- Dev run 1: C2 and C7 failed. Cause, a code defect: on macOS `killpg(pgid, 0)` raises EPERM when the only member left is the unreaped zombie group leader, which crashed the daemon inside `kill_group` (and left the C7 job RUNNING). Fix: reap the leader while waiting and treat EPERM as "only a zombie remains". Dev run 2: 7/7 pass.
- Found during design: cli-agent `run_agent.py` adds `--dangerously-skip-permissions` for claude and agy unless `--isolated` is given. The daemon now passes `--isolated` by default and rejects a non-isolated cli-agent job unless it sets `allow_permission_bypass: true`. C6 gained a fourth case for this (bypass without opt-in). Dev run 3: 7/7 pass.

## Amendment v2 (after the first confirmatory run; criteria and counts unchanged)
- Confirmatory run 1 (frozen `freeze.json`, commit 00a0cda4d): C1 pass (20/20, median 0.005 s, max 0.01 s); C3, C4, C5, C6, C7 pass; **C2 failed**: a trial job did not reach a terminal state within 20 s.
- Diagnosis: the C2 test queued 5 consecutive timeout jobs into one daemon. After the 3rd timeout the circuit breaker opened (`circuit_open`, failures 3), as rail C4 requires, so trials 4-5 stayed QUEUED. The dev run used 1 trial and could not expose this. # Running the Sanctuary Daemon (`running-sanctuary-daemon`)

A deterministic supervisor that never calls a model. It waits on file events (macOS `kqueue`) for job files in `~/.sanctuary/daemon/queue/`, runs each authorized job in its own process group, and records the outcome. Model work happens only inside dispatched jobs, through the companion `cli-agent` (`run_agent.py`, `--isolated` by default).

## Contents
- [Constraints](#constraints) • [Plan a job (interactive)](#plan-a-job-interactive) • [Quick Start](#quick-start) • [Workflow](#workflow) • [Verification](#verification) • [References](#references)

## Constraints
- **Never start it from bootstrap.** Session startup is observational. The human starts the daemon (foreground or a launchd agent); agents only enqueue, read status, and propose `reset`.
- **Human Gate.** Every job needs `authorized_by`. Enqueue only work the human approved in the current context.
- **Daemon states stay in the daemon.** QUEUED/RUNNING/COMPLETED/FAILED/TIMED_OUT/REJECTED and ACTIVE/BLOCKED_ON_HUMAN live in `~/.sanctuary/daemon/`, never in mission manifests.
- **No permission bypass by default.** cli-agent jobs run `--isolated`; a non-isolated job is rejected unless it sets `allow_permission_bypass: true`. `copilot` is refused (work repositories only).
- **Run jobs in a task worktree** (`--cwd .worktrees/<task>`), leased through `manage_coordination.py` as usual.

## Plan a job (interactive)
When the user wants something run in the background, do not enqueue straight away. Follow [plan-job-interview.md](references/plan-job-interview.md):
1. **Check the ground** (read-only): daemon running? circuit closed? leases?
2. **Ask four questions** in plain language: what kind of work, one run or a pipeline (`--after`), which engine (shell, local Qwen, Codex, Antigravity, Claude), which rails (time limit, must commit, worktree, edit permission).
3. **Show a plain-language summary** with the exact command(s) and their cost.
4. **Enqueue only after an explicit "go"**, then confirm with `status` and say how to watch the log.

Say plainly what the daemon cannot do (no retry-until-green loop; isolated claude/agy jobs cannot edit files unless the user approves `--allow-permission-bypass`).

## Quick Start
```bash
D=plugins/sanctuary-core/.apm/skills/running-sanctuary-daemon/scripts/sanctuary_daemon.py
python3 $D run                                   # human: start (foreground)
python3 $D enqueue --mission MISSION-0NN --authorized-by <approver> --timeout 60 --shell "make test"
python3 $D enqueue --mission MISSION-0NN --authorized-by <approver> --timeout 900 --require-commit \
  --cli claude --model claude-opus-5-5 --cwd .worktrees/<task> --instruction "<bounded task>"
python3 $D enqueue --mission MISSION-0NN --authorized-by <approver> --id step-2 --after step-1 --shell "make test"   # pipeline step
python3 $D status
python3 $D reset                                 # human, after reviewing a BLOCKED_ON_HUMAN trip
```

## Workflow
1. Human approves the work and starts the daemon (or it runs under launchd).
2. Agent leases the task and creates its worktree, then enqueues a bounded job with a timeout.
3. The daemon gates the job, dispatches it, enforces the timeout (SIGTERM, 2 s grace, SIGKILL) and records COMPLETED/FAILED/TIMED_OUT.
4. Three consecutive failures put the daemon in BLOCKED_ON_HUMAN; nothing more runs until `reset`.
5. Agent reads `status` and the job log, then continues the normal PR and closeout workflow.

# Sanctuary supervisor daemon: operations

A zero-token outer loop for headless agent runs. It waits on file events for job files, runs each authorized job in its own process group, and enforces timeouts, a failure circuit breaker, policy gates and crash recovery. It never calls a model; models run only inside the jobs it dispatches. Sequence diagram: `sanctuary-daemon-sequence.mmd` in the `operating-sanctuary-guardian` skill's references.

Status: proof of concept, corroborated by MISSION-001 (`LEARNING/experiments/mission-001/`). Stdlib only; macOS `kqueue` watcher with a polling fallback.

## Start it (manual, foreground)

```bash
D=plugins/sanctuary-core/.apm/skills/running-sanctuary-daemon/scripts/sanctuary_daemon.py
python3 $D run                       # Ctrl-C or SIGTERM to stop; state in ~/.sanctuary/daemon/
python3 $D status                    # daemon state and jobs (from another terminal)
```

Queue work (the enqueue is the authorization record; leave `--authorized-by` empty and the job is rejected):

```bash
# deterministic job
python3 $D enqueue --mission MISSION-001 --authorized-by <approver> --timeout 60 --shell "make test"

# agent job through cli-agent (isolated by default: no permission bypass)
python3 $D enqueue --mission MISSION-0NN --authorized-by <approver> --timeout 900 \
  --cli claude --model claude-opus-5-5 --cwd .worktrees/<task> \
  --instruction "Implement X, run the tests, commit with message 'feat: X'." --require-commit
```

Pipelines: `--after <job-id>` makes a job wait for another; it runs only if that job COMPLETED and is otherwise marked SKIPPED. Edits by claude or agy: add `--allow-permission-bypass` (cli-agent jobs only; requires explicit human approval), since isolated `-p` runs cannot edit files.

After 3 consecutive failures the daemon stops dispatching (`BLOCKED_ON_HUMAN`). Review the logs in `~/.sanctuary/daemon/logs/`, then `python3 $D reset`.

## Should session bootstrap start it?

**No.** Start it yourself, or opt in to launchd. Three reasons:

1. **Startup is observational.** Sanctuary's rules keep session startup read-only: it reports state and never starts state-changing work. A daemon that can launch agents which edit and commit is state-changing.
2. **Human Gate.** A bootstrap that starts the dispatcher would let any agent session turn on unattended execution. The daemon should run because you chose to run it.
3. **Lifetime.** A daemon should outlive any one agent session. Tying it to bootstrap would start duplicates (the lock refuses a second one) and stop it when a session ends.

A good later addition (not done here): the boot briefing reports the daemon read-only, for example "daemon: ACTIVE, 2 queued, circuit closed" from `status`.

### Optional: run at login with launchd

Save as `~/Library/LaunchAgents/org.sanctuary.daemon.plist`, replace `<you>` with your user name and adjust paths, then `launchctl load ~/Library/LaunchAgents/org.sanctuary.daemon.plist`. Unload to stop.

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0"><dict>
  <key>Label</key><string>org.sanctuary.daemon</string>
  <key>ProgramArguments</key><array>
    <string>/usr/bin/python3</string>
    <string>/Users/<you>/Projects/Project_Sanctuary/plugins/sanctuary-core/.apm/skills/running-sanctuary-daemon/scripts/sanctuary_daemon.py</string>
    <string>run</string>
  </array>
  <key>RunAtLoad</key><true/>
  <key>KeepAlive</key><true/>
  <key>StandardOutPath</key><string>/Users/<you>/.sanctuary/daemon/launchd.log</string>
  <key>StandardErrorPath</key><string>/Users/<you>/.sanctuary/daemon/launchd.log</string>
</dict></plist>
```

## Rails and what enforces them

| Rail | Enforced by |
|---|---|
| Hard timeout | daemon: SIGTERM to the job's process group, 2 s grace, SIGKILL (and run_agent's own `--timeout`) |
| Failure ceiling | daemon: 3 consecutive FAILED/TIMED_OUT -> BLOCKED_ON_HUMAN until `reset` |
| Authorization | daemon: job needs `authorized_by` |
| Backend policy | daemon: `copilot` refused; bypass flags refused; cli-agent runs `--isolated` unless the job sets `allow_permission_bypass` |
| Worktree boundary, duplicate launch | run_agent `--cwd/--allowed-root`, `--claim-dir/--unit` |
| One daemon at a time | `flock` on `daemon.lock` |
| Crash recovery | on start, jobs left RUNNING are killed and re-queued (max 2 attempts) |

## Known gaps

- `run_agent.py` without `--isolated` adds `--dangerously-skip-permissions` for claude and agy. Isolated claude runs get no edit permission in `-p` mode, so an unattended **editing** run currently needs the explicit bypass opt-in (`enqueue --allow-permission-bypass`).
- No retry-until-green loop; use a fixed `--after` pipeline. A narrower option (`--permission-mode acceptEdits` plus an allowed-tools list) belongs in the companion `cli-agent` skill.
- Claude sign-in tokens expire (the live demo warned of expiry within days); for unattended runs use `claude setup-token`.
- No token budget per job yet: only wall-clock and failure-count rails. A cost rail could read run_agent's `result.json` usage.
- Linux (`inotify`) is untested; the polling fallback is used there.
- One job at a time; no priorities beyond queue order.

`python3 scripts/test_daemon.py` (quick) or `python3 scripts/test_daemon.py --confirm --evidence-dir <dir>` (MISSION-001 trial counts). Protocol and results: `LEARNING/experiments/mission-001/`.
